collection_summary: Anchored-fuzzy geographic instance for the `geographic` query category. The natural-language query 'what countries are commonly considered part of the Middle East' has no objectively correct answer because 'Middle East' is a regionally and politically fuzzy concept; the benchmark therefore anchors to Wikipedia's 'Middle East' article and its primary 'Countries and territory usually considered within the Middle East' list. This commits to a specific definitional choice — the 17 country-status rows the Wikipedia table identifies (16 UN member states plus Palestine, which is a UN observer) — without revealing the source to the LLM under test. The LLM is being measured on whether its parametric notion of 'Middle East' agrees with the cited Wikipedia anchor, not on any personal or alternative definition (UN M49 Western Asia, World Bank MENA, US State Department Bureau of Near Eastern Affairs all give different lists). The Capital(s) column uses the artifact-contract boundary-aware text-field convention with `; ` as the delimiter, so contested or dual capitals (Palestine 'Jerusalem; Ramallah', Yemen 'Sanaa; Aden (provisional)') are recorded honestly without forcing single-label collapse. Result: 17 rows × 3 columns sorted alphabetically by country.
source_coverage_notes: Single-source instance grounded in the Wikipedia 'Middle East' article (Tier B). The Wikipedia table titles itself 'Countries and territory usually considered within the Middle East' and lists 17 country-status rows (Bahrain, Cyprus, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, Yemen) plus Akrotiri and Dhekelia (a British Overseas Territory). Palestine's status in the table is UN observer rather than full member; the other 16 are UN member states. Akrotiri and Dhekelia is excluded here because the natural-language query asks for 'countries' rather than 'countries and territories.' Alternative authoritative anchors give different lists: UN M49 Western Asia (excludes Egypt, includes Caucasus states), World Bank MENA region (broader, includes North Africa), and the CIA World Factbook 'Middle East' region (close to Wikipedia's list but the page returned 403 during this curation). The Wikipedia-anchored 17-row scope is honest about being source_defined rather than exhaustive — it does not claim 'every country considered Middle Eastern by every definition.'
decision_log: 1) Chose query_category=geographic because the query targets a fuzzy spatial concept (Middle East), and the protocol §3 maps such queries to this category. 2) Chose operation_type='filter' to match the artifact-contract expected pairing for geographic queries — the universe is filtered to Middle East members and a few attributes are projected per row. 3) Chose Wikipedia 'Middle East' article (Tier B) over CIA World Factbook (intended Tier C) because the Factbook URL returned 403 during fetch; Wikipedia's article is well-curated, well-cited, and explicitly defines a 'usually considered' canonical list, making it a reasonable anchor for an anchored-fuzzy geographic query. The protocol §4 says Tier C is 'best for' geographic but does not require Tier C exclusively. 4) Excluded Akrotiri and Dhekelia (British Overseas Territory) from the row set because the query asks about 'countries,' not 'countries and territories.' This is documented as a deliberate scope narrowing rather than a Wikipedia error. 5) Applied the artifact-contract Boundary-Aware Fields convention to the Capital column. The Wikipedia source records dual notation for two rows — Palestine ('Jerusalem' and 'Ramallah') and Yemen ('Sanaa' and 'Aden (provisional)') — and a single value for the other 15. Forcing a single label on Palestine would lose the source's deliberate dual notation; the same applies to Yemen's de jure / provisional split during the civil war. The column was renamed to `Capital(s)` with type `text` (not `key`) so the delimited values are explicitly text, and the delimiter `; ` is documented under normalization_decisions. The earlier draft committed to single 'Ramallah' for Palestine and single 'Sanaa' for Yemen; the audit verdict (1 BLOCKING, structural) flagged this as a violation of the boundary-aware pattern, and this revision corrects it. 6) Recorded Israel's capital as the single value 'Jerusalem' per the Wikipedia table (which itself shows only Jerusalem for Israel, despite international recognition being split). Did not unilaterally extend Israel to a dual notation because the source does not support it. The Tel Aviv vs Jerusalem dispute is documented in open_questions rather than reflected in the row. 7) Used canonical full country names ('United Arab Emirates' not 'UAE') per protocol §6. 8) Replaced 'UN member states' wording in temporal_note, _extraction_notes, and source_coverage_notes with the source-table phrasing 'countries and territory usually considered within the Middle East' (or analogues), because Palestine is UN observer rather than member — the prior wording overclaimed.
normalization_decisions: Country names follow country_converter library short_name (v1.3.2) per protocol §6 evaluator-matching rule. 16 of 17 country names match country_converter directly; one row was updated post-source-fetch: 'Turkey' → 'Türkiye' (country_converter adopted the post-2022 UN-recognized rename, while the cited Wikipedia 'Middle East' article still uses 'Turkey'). The evaluator normalizes both LLM output and GT through country_converter, so an LLM that outputs 'Turkey' will still match the GT 'Türkiye'. Other names already canonical: 'United Arab Emirates' not 'UAE', 'Saudi Arabia' not 'KSA', 'Palestine' not 'Palestinian Territories'. The Capital(s) column is a boundary-aware text field with `; ` (semicolon followed by single space) as the delimiter — applied per the artifact-contract Boundary-Aware Fields convention. Single-value rows store one city name; dual-value rows store both with the delimiter (e.g., Palestine: 'Jerusalem; Ramallah'; Yemen: 'Sanaa; Aden (provisional)'). The Yemen row preserves the source's '(provisional)' qualifier inline. City names are bare (no country qualifier; 'Riyadh' not 'Riyadh, Saudi Arabia'). Population values are bare integers in persons, no commas, no 'million' suffix, per protocol §6. The Wikipedia table uses comma-separated populations (e.g., '109,450,000') which were stripped to bare integers (109450000). Sort order is country ASC for stable presentation. Population estimates come from heterogeneous years (mostly 2025; Lebanon and Palestine 2024; Syria 2010). Heterogeneity is documented in temporal_note rather than reflected in a per-row 'estimate year' column to keep the schema compact.
open_questions: 1) Israel's capital recognition is internationally disputed. The cited Wikipedia table records 'Jerusalem' as a single value (no boundary-aware dual notation in the source for Israel), so the row commits to Jerusalem. The LLM under test may give Tel Aviv (where many embassies are located) and would be scored as wrong against this row. This is a known artifact of source-grounded curation against a politically contested fact and is consistent with how the benchmark tests parametric agreement with a specific source. 2) Syria's 2010 population is 16 years out of date relative to the 2026-04-27 access; current estimates differ by ~5–8 million depending on how internal displacement and refugee returns are counted. The 2010 figure is what Wikipedia retains as the last census-anchored estimate. 3) The 'Middle East' country set is fuzzy — alternative authoritative definitions (UN M49 Western Asia excludes Egypt; World Bank MENA includes North Africa; US State Department Bureau of Near Eastern Affairs has a different list) would yield different rows. The 17-country Wikipedia 'usually considered' set is one defensible commitment among several. 4) The protocol target for `geographic` is 5 instances; this is the first. Future siblings could anchor to alternative definitions of fuzzy regions (Pacific Northwest, Sahel, Central Europe, Latin America) to test category-internal definitional variance. 5) Country names validated against country_converter short_name (v1.3.2). One row updated: 'Turkey' → 'Türkiye'. Other 16 already canonical. See normalization_decisions for the choice and rationale.
